title: How to Build Stronger Engineering Teams With Values (November 2026)
summary: How Dover's engineering team puts six company values into practice, from ownership to fast shipping. Updated November 2026.
body_markdown:
To[build stronger engineering teams with values](https://www.dover.com/) , the values have to show up in daily habits. Company values often sit on a careers page long before anyone on an engineering team can say how they change a code review, a sprint plan, or a hiring decision. Early-stage teams tend to write them down once headcount makes informal culture harder to pass along, and the useful versions point to specific habits instead of adjectives. The six values below each come with the engineering practice that makes it concrete, from scheduled tech debt work to publicly crediting teammates.


**TLDR:**


- Strong engineering culture requires deliberate practices like monthly Reliability Days to reduce tech debt.
- Shipping fast and iterating beats waiting for perfection; teams move faster when feedback loops stay short.
- Growth path matters more than starting experience; engineers can expand into full-stack work quickly with the right support.
- Publicly crediting teammates and celebrating wins builds genuine connection, even across distributed teams.
- One startup engineering team formalized six values as it scaled from 5 to 35 people (as of 2021) to preserve the culture built during early growth.


Value What it means at Dover How the EPD team practices it


Ownership Take responsibility for results and drive projects to completion Three-day Reliability Days each month for tech debt; asking for help early


Intellectual Honesty Reason from first principles and draw conclusions from facts and data Close code review on every pull request before shipping


Big Picture Thinking Optimize for the long-term good of the business over team interests Design docs that scope requirements before implementation starts


Gotta Go Fast Bias toward action and identify the MVP Ship functionally complete versions first, then iterate on feedback


Slope over Y-intercept Good ideas can come from anyone, and people who do great work grow fastest Full-stack expectations for every engineer and a weekly reading group


Active Generosity Make time for each other and celebrate contributions Crediting every contributor during company-wide updates


## Ownership


At Dover, when we see a problem or an opportunity, we never think “that’s not my job”. We take responsibility for our results, both successes and failures. We drive projects to completion, even if it means doing unglamorous work or work that’s outside of our job description.


### How We Practice Ownership on the EPD Team


Unglamorous work is going to be a part of any startup job, and something highly valuable for us are our Reliability Days. When I started, we had a Reliability Day every other Wednesday, focused strictly on[paying down tech debt](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TechnicalDebt.html) . Today, Reliability Days happen three days in a row, once a month, giving us more time to finish tasks that a single day never allowed. It’s not as glamorous as feature work, but we care so much about our code quality, longevity, and maintainability that we dedicate team time to it, refactoring code, improving monitoring, and making our systems better for everyone. I actually get excited for Reliability Days now, because it’s rewarding to see the improvements we make when we set the time aside for them.


On the EPD team, we also practice ownership by taking responsibility for seeking help when we need it. As a new hire, I had the usual hesitation: *“am I asking too many questions, should I already know this?”* In my first one-on-one, Max (our CEO as of 2021) told me to assume I wasn’t asking *enough* questions, since asking too many wasn’t possible. Noa (one of our Engineers) was my onboarding buddy, and he told me no question is too small. From day one, we’re “teaching people how to fish”. Google’s[team effectiveness research](https://rework.withgoogle.com/intl/en/guides/understand-team-effectiveness) ranks psychological safety first among the factors behind effective teams, and feeling free to ask a basic question is part of it.


## Intellectual Honesty


At Dover, we are intellectually rigorous and reason from first-principles. We’re very open to trying things out and running experiments. We believe it’s okay to be wrong, because learning is valuable and helps us get to our ultimate goal. We make conclusions based on facts and data. We’re truthful with ourselves even if the conclusions are inconvenient or make us look bad.


### How We Practice Intellectual Honesty on the EPD Team


On the Eng team, every pull request gets reviewed before shipping to production, a practice Google’s[code review standard](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/standard.html) ties to improving overall code health. There have been times when a review has stung, when none of my code felt like it was in good shape, but I value getting feedback from teammates with more experience and different perspectives than me. That constant feedback has improved our team’s code quality overall, and it helps all of us build a thicker skin and take feedback less personally. There’s a sense of humility on the Eng team, where people stay open to feedback and there are no big egos.


## Big Picture Thinking


At Dover, we optimize for what’s good for the business, long-term, over our individual/team-level interests. We’re not territorial; we avoid politics and gatekeeping. We think through externalities and the long-term implications of decisions that we make. Instead of doing things as one-offs, we build processes and playbooks.


### How We Practice Big Picture Thinking on the EPD Team


On the EPD team, we’re constantly thinking about the long term, both for our customers and for internal users like Engagement Managers and Customer Support. We build features with their day-to-day work in mind.


With Eng decisions, we always ask ourselves: *how is this going to be used in the long term?* We structure things with scalability in mind. Right now I’m scoping a[design doc](https://www.industrialempathy.com/posts/design-docs-at-google/) for reworking our onboarding flow, meeting with multiple people to gather requirements before writing a line of code. It’s tempting to jump straight into implementation, but a thorough upfront understanding of the problem and solution saves us time later.


## Gotta Go Fast


At Dover, we bias towards action. We value output and results over face-time. We are deliberate in identifying the MVP and are comfortable cutting the right corners.


### How We Practice Gotta Go Fast on the EPD Team


On the EPD team, we believe in shipping things functionally complete, even if the first version doesn’t match the design specs. Speed first means I get feedback sooner and deliver value more quickly.


“Gotta go fast” gets repeated all the time on the Eng team. I can be detail-focused, and I want to get things right before putting them out there, but I’ve learned it’s okay if it’s not right the first time. We’re constantly reviewing each other’s code, so it’s safe to move fast.


## Slope Over Y-Intercept


At Dover, we value experience, but don’t discount people who don’t have it. We believe good ideas can come from anywhere and anyone. People who do great work grow the fastest. The business needs them and pulls them into new areas.


### How We Practice Slope Over Y-Intercept on the EPD Team


Coming from a creative agency, most of my development experience had been focused in frontend. At Dover, we’re expected to touch all areas of development: frontend, backend, and infrastructure. It was intimidating at first, but the supportive nature of our team helped me jump into full stack work in my first couple days here. Three months in, as of 2021, I have far more confidence in areas that felt rusty when I started. The Eng team even has a weekly reading group where we read and discuss Eng books together, and that constant exposure to new problems and ideas keeps work exciting!


## Active Generosity


At Dover, we make time for each other, whether it means getting to know someone personally or helping them up-level in a new area. We are enthusiastic about acknowledging and celebrating each other’s contributions, both 1:1 and publicly. We have a sense of humor about ourselves, and take things lightly. You should be able to laugh at yourself.


### How We Practice Active Generosity on the EPD Team


This was the value I really felt during my interview process, and it drew me in to Dover. Friends of mine who joined other remote teams this year often feel disconnected and don’t know anyone they work with.


As of 2021, I’m based in New York with a few other Dover employees, but most of our team is in SF. I still haven’t even met anyone in person yet, but I feel like I’ve actually made friends. Everyone is enthusiastic about celebrating each other’s wins.


During company-wide meetings, DRIs for our projects present their work and credit every single person who helped them ship it. People love shining a light on each other’s work, and we’re always saying thank you.


## Where These Values Stand in 2026


Dover has grown since this post was written in 2021. The product now pairs a free ATS and[AI recruiting features](https://www.dover.com/ai) with a Premium plan and a marketplace of fractional recruiters, and in 2026 Dover launched[Dover Startup Jobs](https://jobs.dover.com/) , a free job board for venture-backed startups. Dover is also the layer fractional recruiting agencies are built on, and each recruiter in the marketplace carries verified reviews from the founders who hired them. The six values described above have stayed the same.


Engineering work has changed too. In the[2026 Stack Overflow Developer Survey](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2026/ai) , 66% cited coding assistants and agents as a use of AI, and 48% said they trust AI output when they can easily verify it. When more code starts as an AI-assisted draft, Ownership and Intellectual Honesty carry more weight, since close code review and clear responsibility for what ships matter whether a teammate or a tool wrote the first version. For founders making their[first engineering hire](https://www.dover.com/blog/how-to-hire-first-engineer) , writing these values down early gives every new teammate a shared reference point.


## How Dover Supports Hiring Engineers Who Fit Your Values


Values only shape a team if the hiring process can assess for them. Dover’s free ATS lets a team build customizable interview plans and use feedback forms to collect interviewer input at each stage, so qualities like Ownership and Intellectual Honesty get assessed against the same questions, in line with[interview process best practices](https://www.dover.com/blog/interview-scorecard-guide) , instead of whichever interviewer happens to be in the room.


An ATS gives hiring structure, but it doesn’t add sourcing capacity. For a team making one or two engineering hires a year, a founder[sourcing candidates](https://www.dover.com/blog/candidate-sourcing-techniques-guide) directly in the ATS is often enough. When a role is senior or specialized, or no one has hours for outreach, a[fractional recruiter](https://www.dover.com/blog/what-is-a-fractional-recruiter-guide) can plug in on top of the same ATS. Recruiters in Dover’s marketplace have worked at startups and with early-stage founders, carry verified reviews from the founders who hired them, and work inside the shared pipeline, so hiring managers can see sourcing activity and candidate flow as it happens. Dover is also the layer fractional recruiting agencies are built on, so the values conversation and the candidate record can stay in one system whether a founder works with an independent recruiter or an agency.


## FAQs


### How did Dover’s engineering team decide which values to formalize as it scaled from 5 to 35 people?


Dover didn’t design its values from scratch. The team identified principles that had already shaped how people worked and made them explicit as headcount grew. Writing them down gave new hires a shared reference point from day one, which matters most when a team is adding people faster than culture can spread through informal observation.


### What are “Reliability Days” and how do engineering teams use them to manage tech debt?


Reliability Days are dedicated blocks of time. At Dover, that means three consecutive days each month focused solely on paying down tech debt, refactoring code, improving monitoring, and strengthening the codebase without feature work competing for attention. Teams that schedule this consistently tend to make more progress than teams that tackle debt reactively.


### Should engineering values cover AI-assisted code the same way they cover human-written code?


Yes, and the bar may need to be higher. When more code starts as an AI-generated draft, values like Ownership and Intellectual Honesty carry more practical weight. Close code review, clear accountability for what ships, and a willingness to question output matter whether a teammate or a tool wrote the first version. The review process doesn’t change; what changes is that skipping it carries more risk.


### Do I need a recruiter if I already use an ATS?


Not always. An ATS organizes the pipeline, interview plans, and feedback, but it doesn’t source candidates or run outreach. Teams making a few hires a year can often manage with the ATS alone, while senior or specialized engineering roles, or a team with no recruiting bandwidth, may call for a fractional recruiter. When that recruiter works inside the same ATS, the hiring team typically keeps real-time visibility into the pipeline and avoids duplicate outreach.


## Final Thoughts on Company Values and Engineering Team Culture


To[build stronger engineering teams with values](https://www.dover.com/) , put them in routines a new hire can see in the first week: a scheduled block for tech debt, code review that treats feedback as information, a habit of crediting the people who helped. The right mix varies with team size and stage, and Dover’s own six values grew out of practices that existed before anyone wrote them down. Dover’s free ATS offers customizable interview plans and feedback forms, so those same values can carry into how a team assesses its next hire. Written values tend to hold when the habits behind them are specific enough to repeat.
